result: The authors present a novel method for extracting and separating excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances at high temporal resolution from single-neuron intracellular recordings in rhythmically active networks. The method extends previous approaches and is claimed to be applicable to various experimental setups and rhythmic circuits.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the method is 'novel and potentially powerful' and 'described well,' but express significant concerns about 'several untested assumptions underlying the approach.' The anonymous reviewer specifically questions whether the method can 'essentially deconvolve the underlying conductance changes' without voltage-clamp data at multiple command voltages, stating 'I am concerned that this simply may not be possible.' This indicates the core methodological claims remain uncertain despite the quality of the work.

result: The authors claim that phase-specific current-voltage dependencies are almost perfectly linear across a wide voltage range (-100 to -60 mV), where voltage-gated ion channels are closed and do not significantly contribute to neuronal I-V relationships.
evaluation: While the reviewer acknowledges 'the authors present evidence that the I-V relationship is linear over most of the voltage range examined, and this is a helpful addition,' they raise fundamental concerns about the assumption of linear I-V for synaptic conductances. The reviewer notes that 'open rectification will be a feature of any conductance generated by asymmetric distributions of ions' and questions 'how the extraction of information concerning the excitatory and inhibitory conductances relies on the assumption of a linear I-V for these conductances,' indicating uncertainty about whether linearity holds for the synaptic conductances themselves.

result: The authors characterize synaptic conductance patterns for six different respiratory neuron types (pre-I/I, ramp-I, early-I, late-I, post-I, and aug-E), including their excitatory and inhibitory inputs across respiratory phases, with immunohistochemical identification of inhibitory neuron subtypes.
evaluation: While reviewers do not directly critique the specific conductance patterns observed, the anonymous reviewer raises a fundamental limitation: 'descending control from the Pons and the neocortex will not be contributing much to the synaptic drive and ascending information from respiratory muscles will also be absent completely.' The reviewer argues this limitation 'does need to be considered when using an approach of this type to speculate on the prevalence of specific circuit motifs within the medulla,' suggesting the characterization may not reflect complete circuit function.

result: The authors validate their method by showing that conductance profiles extracted from current-clamp and voltage-clamp recordings are very similar in shape and relationship, and that profiles remain consistent across different reversal potential values and recording epochs.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer expresses concern that previous approaches 'involved the recording of transmembrane current changes during visual stimulation that were undertaken in voltage-clamp at various command voltages to estimate the underlying conductance changes,' whereas the current method attempts to extract conductances without this information. The reviewer states 'I am concerned that this simply may not be possible,' which casts doubt on the validation approach despite the comparative data presented.

result: The authors report that inhibitory synaptic reversal potentials varied significantly among cells (-62 to -116 mV), which they attribute to electrode distance from synaptic inputs, while maintaining that timing estimates remain reliable.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about reversal potential variability or the reliability of timing estimates. The claims are based on established literature (Calvin, 1969; Spruston et al., 1993; Wehr and Zador, 2003) and no concerns were raised about this aspect of the methodology.

result: The authors conclude that phasic excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs shape membrane potential trajectories and spiking patterns throughout the respiratory cycle, with profiles consistent with the network architecture proposed by Smith et al., 2007.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer specifically cautions that the experimental preparation limitation 'does need to be considered when using an approach of this type to speculate on the prevalence of specific circuit motifs within the medulla.' This directly challenges the interpretation of network architecture and interactions, as the in situ preparation lacks supra-brainstem and peripheral inputs that would be present in vivo.

result: The authors claim that total conductance has static and dynamic components, and that the linear upper boundary observed in wedge diagrams implies neurons receive only inhibitory input during certain respiratory phases.
evaluation: While reviewers do not directly address these specific claims, the anonymous reviewer's fundamental concern about the linear I-V assumption and whether conductances can be deconvolved without voltage-clamp data at multiple command voltages undermines confidence in these theoretical interpretations derived from the method.

result: The authors acknowledge that their profiles of neuronal synaptic interactions are specific to the in situ reduced rat brainstem-spinal cord system and cannot account for supra-brainstem and peripheral circuit inputs in vivo.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly states this limitation should be discussed, noting 'descending control from the Pons and the neocortex will not be contributing much to the synaptic drive and ascending information from respiratory muscles will also be absent completely.' The authors' acknowledgment of this limitation is appropriate and aligns with reviewer concerns.

result: The authors describe methodological details including respiratory cycle period (3-4 s), time resolution (1/300 of period), data selection criteria, experimental preparation, and ethical approval.
evaluation: The editor notes 'the electrophysiological techniques and results are of high quality,' and reviewers do not challenge these methodological details. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges 'this data-driven approach to explore neural circuits is described well in this study.'
